title: Linear algebra
text:
A mixed strategy is a probability vector over pure actions. If player \(i\) has \(m\) pure actions, a mixed strategy is
\[
\Delta^{m-1}=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^m:\; x_k\ge 0\;\forall k,\;\sum_{k=1}^m x_k = 1\right\},
\]
the \((m-1)\)-simplex.
Intuition. You can think of \(x\) as a “weighting” of actions. The simplex condition just says: nonnegative weights that sum to 1.

title: Linear algebra
text:
Payoff matrices and expected payoff
In a two-player normal-form game, let player 1 have \(m\) actions and player 2 have \(n\) actions. Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be player 1’s payoff matrix (and \(B\) for player 2). If player 1 plays \(x\in\Delta^{m-1}\) and player 2 plays \(y\in\Delta^{n-1}\), then player 1’s expected payoff is
\[
u_1(x,y)=x^\top A y.
\]
Intuition. First compute expected payoffs against each of player 2’s pure actions (\(Ay\)). Then average those numbers using player 1’s mixing weights (\(x^\top\)).

title: Linear algebra
text:
Example: 2×2 game
Suppose
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}
2 & 0\\
1 & 3
\end{pmatrix},\quad
x=\begin{pmatrix}0.4\\0.6\end{pmatrix},\quad
y=\begin{pmatrix}0.25\\0.75\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Compute
\[
Ay=
\begin{pmatrix}
2 & 0\\
1 & 3
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
0.25\\0.75
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
0.5\\
2.5
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
u_1(x,y)=x^\top(Ay)=0.4\cdot 0.5+0.6\cdot 2.5=1.7.
\]
So the mixed-vs-mixed expected payoff is \(1.7\) for player 1.

title: Probability
text:
A mixed strategy is a probability distribution over actions. If the action set is finite, this is just a probability vector (see the simplex definition in Linear algebra).
Intuition. “Randomizing” in game theory is not mystical: it’s a distribution that other players can form beliefs about.

title: Probability
text:
Expectation
If a random variable \(X\) takes values \(x_k\) with probabilities \(p_k\), then
\[
\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_k x_k p_k.
\]
In games, expected utility under a mixed strategy is exactly this idea: average the payoff over all possible outcomes, weighted by their probabilities.

title: Probability
text:
Bayes’ rule
For events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\),
\[
\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\frac{\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\,\mathbb{P}(A)}{\mathbb{P}(B)}.
\]
Intuition. Prior belief \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) gets updated by how well \(A\) predicts the evidence \(B\).

title: Probability
text:
Example: updating beliefs about types
A player is either type \(H\) or \(L\). Prior \(\mathbb{P}(H)=0.3\), \(\mathbb{P}(L)=0.7\). You observe a signal \(s\). Suppose
\[
\mathbb{P}(s\mid H)=0.8,\qquad \mathbb{P}(s\mid L)=0.2.
\]
First compute the overall likelihood of \(s\):
\[
\mathbb{P}(s)=\mathbb{P}(s\mid H)\mathbb{P}(H)+\mathbb{P}(s\mid L)\mathbb{P}(L)=0.8\cdot 0.3+0.2\cdot 0.7=0.38.
\]
Then the posterior belief is
\[
\mathbb{P}(H\mid s)=\frac{0.8\cdot 0.3}{0.38}\approx 0.6316.
\]
So after observing \(s\), belief in type \(H\) rises from \(0.3\) to about \(0.63\).

title: Optimization
text:
A best response is an optimization problem. Given others’ strategies \(s_{-i}\), player \(i\) chooses
\[
BR_i(s_{-i})\in \arg\max_{s_i\in S_i} u_i(s_i,s_{-i}).
\]
Intuition. A Nash equilibrium is a fixed point of best responses: everyone is already choosing an argmax given others.

title: Optimization
text:
FOC / SOC (unconstrained)
If \(f\) is differentiable and you maximize over an interval, an interior optimum \(x^*\) satisfies the first-order condition (FOC)
\[
f'(x^*)=0.
\]
If \(f\) is twice differentiable, the second-order condition (SOC) for a local maximum is
\[
f''(x^*)<0.
\]
Intuition. FOC finds stationary points; SOC checks that the curve bends downward.

title: Optimization
text:
KKT conditions (constrained)
For maximizing \(f(x)\) subject to inequality constraints \(g_j(x)\le 0\), define the Lagrangian
\[
\mathcal{L}(x,\lambda)=f(x)-\sum_{j}\lambda_j g_j(x),
\qquad \lambda_j\ge 0.
\]
KKT conditions (at an optimum, under standard regularity assumptions) include: - Stationarity: \(\nabla_x \mathcal{L}(x^*,\lambda^*)=0\) - Primal feasibility: \(g_j(x^*)\le 0\) - Dual feasibility: \(\lambda_j^*\ge 0\) - Complementary slackness: \(\lambda_j^* g_j(x^*)=0\) for all \(j\)
Intuition. Constraints either bind (then they get a positive “shadow price” \(\lambda_j\)) or don’t bind (then \(\lambda_j=0\)).

title: Optimization
section: Example: best response with a constraint
text:
Example: best response with a constraint
Maximize \(f(x)=2x-x^2\) subject to \(x\ge 0\).
Write the constraint as \(g(x)=-x\le 0\). Lagrangian:
\[
\mathcal{L}(x,\lambda)= (2x-x^2)-\lambda(-x)=2x-x^2+\lambda x.
\]
KKT: - Stationarity: \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x}=2-2x+\lambda=0\) - Primal feasibility: \(x\ge 0\) - Dual feasibility: \(\lambda\ge 0\) - Complementary slackness: \(\lambda x=0\)
From stationarity: \(2-2x+\lambda=0 \Rightarrow x=1+\lambda/2\).
If \(x>0\), then complementary slackness implies \(\lambda=0\), so \(x=1\). Check feasibility: \(1\ge 0\) yes. So the solution is \(x^*=1\).
(If the unconstrained maximizer had been negative, the constraint would bind and you’d get \(x^*=0\) with \(\lambda>0\).)
